🦉Did You Know? 

Leonard Wood: The Forgotten Hero Behind the Rough Riders ⚕️⭐

Meet the man who actually commanded the Rough Riders: Leonard Wood, a Harvard-trained Army surgeon turned battlefield leader.

Born in 1860, Wood earned the Medal of Honor in the 1880s for extraordinary bravery during the Geronimo campaign in Arizona — riding through hostile territory and leading troops under fire. 

In 1898, he partnered with his friend Theodore Roosevelt to raise the 1st U.S. Volunteer Cavalry. Wood served as Colonel, with Roosevelt as his second-in-command. He led the regiment in Cuba at Las Guasimas and helped secure victory at San Juan Heights before being promoted to Brigadier General on the spot — handing day-to-day command of the Rough Riders to Roosevelt.

Beyond Cuba, Wood served as Military Governor of Cuba (improving public health and supporting yellow fever research), governed in the Philippines, and later became U.S. Army Chief of Staff — the only physician ever to hold that role. 

A true soldier-statesman who blended medicine, courage, and leadership. Wood’s story shows how the Rough Riders legend was built on real expertise and partnership.

🇺🇸250 Years of American Heroes🇺🇸

Teddy Roosevelt’s Rough Riders: The Wildest Volunteer Cavalry in American History

In 1898, as war erupted with Spain over Cuba, Theodore Roosevelt ditched his desk job as Assistant Secretary of the Navy to create one of the most colorful fighting units ever — the 1st U.S. Volunteer Cavalry, forever known as the Rough Riders.
This wasn’t a typical army regiment. Roosevelt recruited a wild mix of:
•  Tough cowboys, miners & ranchers from the West
•  Ivy League athletes, polo players & Eastern elites
•  Native Americans, lawmen & even a few former outlaws
They trained in Texas, then shipped to Cuba… but left most of their horses behind. They became “Wood’s Weary Walkers” — fighting on foot.

Their Legendary Charge:
On July 1, 1898, at the Battle of San Juan Hill (starting with Kettle Hill), Lt. Col. Roosevelt led a daring uphill assault under heavy Spanish fire. Pistol in hand, he rallied his men forward in one of the most famous charges in U.S. military history. The Rough Riders captured the heights, helping secure victory in Cuba. 

The unit only fought for a few intense months, but their bravery made Roosevelt a national hero and paved his path to the White House.

Rough Riders: proof that unlikely brothers — cowboys riding with Harvard grads — could become legends when it counted.
